# FDG3075

> DO use two parameters named *sender* and *e* in event handlers.

Framework Design Guidelines, 3rd edition, section 3.6.3 Names of Events.

## How it is checked

- Check: fdg (partial coverage)
- Diagnostics: FDG3075
- Automatic fix: not applied automatically (the fix can break callers)
- Severity: library warning, application warning, test none
- Status: verified

Message: Name the two parameters of the event handler '{0}' 'sender' and 'e'

FDG3075 reports an externally visible delegate that an event in the same compilation uses, or whose name ends with 'EventHandler', when its parameters are not exactly 'sender' and 'e'. Parameter types are not checked. Renaming or changing the parameters of a public delegate changes the public API (Appendix D.11.1), so the fix is breaking; FDG3075 has no code fix.

## From the book

The sender parameter represents the object that raised the event. The sender parameter is typically of type `object`, even if it is possible to employ a more specific type. The pattern is used consistently across .NET and is described in more detail in section 5.4.

> **Jeremy Barton:** The `object sender` parameter may be my least favorite guideline in .NET. But, for consistency, I have followed it in every event I’ve ever declared.

```csharp
public delegate void <EventName>EventHandler(object sender,
                                             <EventName>EventArgs e);
```
